payload.answer:
DISEÑO EXPERIMENTAL FINAL — "Criticality of dynamic context memory lookup and unit representations for InfLLM in long-context tasks" (DISEÑO PLANIFICATORIO)

0) DECLARACIÓN (punto 4 del brief)
NO se ha ejecutado ningún experimento. Este documento es un diseño planificatorio, conforme al brief ("Do not claim that an experiment was run"; track.md: "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required"). El workspace no contiene código de InfLLM; toda ejecución presupone infraestructura externa con GPU.

1) PREGUNTA DE INVESTIGACIÓN Y OBJETIVO
Cuantificar qué tan críticos son (A) la memoria de contexto dinámica con recuperación (lookup) y (B) la elección de la representación/granularidad de las unidades, para el rendimiento de InfLLM en contexto largo, mediante un diseño factorial de ablation con presupuesto de KV emparejado, sobre una suite de benchmarks de contexto largo.

2) JUSTIFICACIÓN DEL DISEÑO
- Factorial 2 componentes: aísla el efecto principal de cada factor y su interacción, evitando confundir "recuperar más contexto" con "mejores unidades".
- Niveles de control (sin-lookup/recencia; lookup aleatorio) separan el efecto de la POLÍTICA de recuperación del mero hecho de tener memoria comprimida.
- Baselines de eviction con presupuesto igualado (H2O, StreamingLLM, SnapKV) sitúan a InfLLM frente a la misma clase funcional (compresión de KV con presupuesto), de modo que la "criticidad" se juzga frente al estado del arte, no solo frente a ablations internas.
- Full KV-cache como oráculo superior (límite de eficiencia).
- Diseño emparejado (mismos prompts en todas las condiciones) maximiza potencia estadística.
- RULER (sintético, control de longitud, multi-query retrieval) como primario; NIAH para profundidad de recuperación; LongBench para validez externa.

3) CONDICIONES EXPERIMENTALES
3.1 Modelo e infraestructura (supuestos, §8): modelo base primario LLaMA-3 8B (Instruct); FP16; decodificación determinista (temp=0), salvo subconjunto QA de LongBench (3 semillas, promedio). Infraestructura: 4×A100/H100 80 GB; fallback 1 GPU. Sin fine-tuning (InfLLM opera en inferencia).
3.2 Factor A — mecanismo de memoria/lookup (5 niveles):
  A0 full-context (oráculo, sin compresión);
  A1 InfLLM completo (memoria dinámica + lookup top-k_r por paso);
  A2 InfLLM sin lookup: recencia estática (unidad más cercana a la posición de generación);
  A3 InfLLM con lookup aleatorio (k_r unidades uniformes; control de política);
  A4 baselines de eviction con presupuesto igualado: H2O, StreamingLLM, SnapKV (opcional; 3 condiciones).
3.3 Factor B — representación/granularidad de unidades (4 niveles, aplicable a A1–A3):
  B1 chunks fijos de 128 tokens; B2 unidades por oración; B3 unidades por párrafo/sección; B4 unidades jerárquicas/semánticas (estilo InfLLM-v2). Subvariante secundaria: embedding de resumen vs. embedding crudo (en B2 y B4).
  Factorial completo: A1×B1–B4, A2×B1–B4, A3×B1–B4 = 12 condiciones InfLLM + A0 + 3 eviction = 16 condiciones.
3.4 Benchmarks y escalera de longitudes:
  - Escalera: 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K (core); 1M (extendido, solo A1–A4).
  - RULER (primario; 6 subtasks × 128 prompts/longitud): factorial completo en 8K, 32K, 128K; spot-checks en 4K/16K/64K (solo A1×B4 + A0 + A4).
  - NIAH (128 profundidades/longitud): 8K–128K + 1M.
  - LongBench (~500 prompts): celdas 4K–32K.
  - IDs de prompt fijos y compartidos entre todas las condiciones (diseño emparejado).
3.5 Evaluación: RULER por exact match; NIAH por precisión de recuperación (posición exacta); LongBench por EM/F1 por tarea. Diagnósticos: recall@k_r del lookup (unidades recuperadas vs. unidades que contienen la respuesta), KV residente medido (MiB reales, no nominales), latencia por paso.

4) CONTROLES
4.1 Definición operativa de equivalencia de presupuesto KV (punto 1 solicitado)
Definición: K_tok = número de entradas de KV a nivel de token residentes en cualquier instante de la inferencia (K+V, todas las capas, FP16).
  - InfLLM: K_tok = m·u (m unidades en memoria × u tokens/unidad) → para cada presupuesto K: m = ⌊K/u⌋.
  - H2O: K_tok = W_recent + K_top (ventana recencia + top-importancia).
  - StreamingLLM: K_tok = W + s (ventana + sink tokens).
  - SnapKV: K_tok = K_snap (presupuesto comprimido).
Restricción: para cada K ∈ {8K, 16K, 32K, 64K}, todos los métodos operan con K_tok = K ± 2%. Los niveles A2/A3 comparten el mismo m que A1 (huella idéntica; solo cambia la política), aislando el efecto del lookup.
Diagnóstico secundario (atención por paso): A(InfLLM) = k_r·u vs. A(baseline) = K; se reporta la razón A/K. Análisis de sensibilidad "compute-matched": StreamingLLM con W = k_r·u (misma atención por paso) para disociar presupuesto de atención de huella de memoria.
4.2 Otros controles: mismo modelo y tokenizer en todas las condiciones; prompts y decodificación idénticos; semillas fijas; KV residente medido experimentalmente; prefill con batching idéntico; presupuesto de memoria verificado por log, no solo por configuración.

5) PLAN DE ANÁLISIS ESTADÍSTICO (punto 2 solicitado)
5.1 Unidad de análisis y modelo: resultado binario a nivel de prompt, emparejado entre condiciones. Modelo principal: logístico multinivel: logit(p) = f(lookup, unit, lookup×unit) + (1|benchmark) + (1|benchmark:prompt); longitud como estrato (y análisis agregado con covariada log-longitud). Estimaciones reportadas en escala de probabilidad: RD (risk difference, en pp) con IC 95% por bootstrap de clúster (10.000 resamples, re-muestreo de prompts dentro de benchmark) + OR del modelo mixto.
5.2 Contrastes:
  Δlookup (primario C1): RD(A1 − A2) a nivel B4, agregado sobre longitudes; secundario: a cada nivel de unidad y por longitud. Descomposición: RD(A1 − A3) = efecto total de la política de recuperación; RD(A3 − A2) = sesgo de posición/recencia.
  Δunit (primario C2): RD(B4 − B1) con lookup completo (B1 fijado a priori como referencia de mejor chunk fijo).
  Interacción A×B (primario C3): difference-in-differences Δlookup(B4) − Δlookup(B1) con IC 95%, más el término de interacción del modelo mixto (OR, IC 95%).
5.3 Múltiples comparaciones: familia primaria {C1, C2, C3} → Holm-Bonferroni (α=0.05); familia secundaria (contrastes pairwise de unidades, Δlookup por longitud) → Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q=0.05.
5.4 Potencia: diseño emparejado con n ≈ 768–1280 prompts/celda (RULER 768/longitud; +NIAH 128; +LongBench 500 en la celda 32K). Con 25% de discordancia entre condiciones: RD detectable ≈ 4.4 pp (n=768) a ≈ 3.4 pp (n=1280), α=0.05 bilateral, potencia 0.80; análisis agregado sobre 3 longitudes (n≈2304) → ≈ 2.5 pp.
5.5 Regla de decisión sobre criticidad (pre-registrada):
  - |RD| ≥ 5 pp y IC 95% ∌ 0 → componente "CRÍTICO".
  - 2–5 pp y IC 95% ∌ 0 → "IMPORTANTE".
  - IC 95% ∋ 0 o < 2 pp → "NO DEMOSTRADO".
  Corroboraciones: (i) si acc(A2) < acc(A4) a K igualado, el lookup es el componente diferenciador (sin él, InfLLM queda por debajo de un baseline de eviction simple); (ii) ratio oráculo acc(A1)/acc(A0) por longitud (frente de eficiencia); (iii) si la IC de C3 ∌ 0 → "la criticidad del lookup depende de la representación de unidades". Conclusión final: matriz de veredictos (lookup × representación de unidades) + interacción.

6) FACTIBILIDAD (punto 3 solicitado)
6.1 Cálculo de KV: KV_bytes = 2 · L · H_kv · d_head · 2B · seq_len.
  - LLaMA-3 8B (L=32, H_kv=8, d=128): 128 KiB/token → 128K = 16 GiB; 1M = 128 GiB.
  - LLaMA-3 70B (L=80, H_kv=8, d=128): 320 KiB/token → 128K = 40 GiB; 1M = 320 GiB.
6.2 Rango máximo realista y manejo del oráculo:
  - Core: 4K–128K. El oráculo a 128K es viable en 8B con 80 GB (16 GiB KV + 16 GiB pesos + activaciones ≈ 50 GiB); 192K también viable (24 GiB KV); 256K en límite.
  - 1M: el oráculo es INVIALE en 80 GB (128 GiB). Manejo: (i) la brecha frente al oráculo se reporta solo hasta la longitud máxima viable (128K); (ii) a 1M se ejecutan solo A1–A4 (KV residente = K, p. ej., 32K → 4 GiB; prefill en chunks), con n reducido a 128 prompts; (iii) para el subtask de recuperación a 1M, NIAH ground-truth actúa como oráculo proxy; (iv) upper bound analítico: ajustar acc(A0)(L) sobre la escalera 16K–128K (decaimiento log-lineal o logístico), extrapolar a 1M con intervalo de predicción 95%, etiquetado explícitamente como ESTIMACIÓN, nunca como medición.
6.3 Estimación de cómputo: core = 16 condiciones × ~3.2K prompts ≈ 51.000 prompt-runs; tiempo medio ponderado por longitud ≈ 40 s (8B, A100) ≈ 550–650 GPU-horas ≈ 6–8 GPU-días en 4×A100 (incluye iteración). Extendido (1M): 4 condiciones × 128 prompts × 2–5 min ≈ 10–40 GPU-horas. Fallback 1 GPU: core reducido a 32K y 128K (~2–3 semanas).

7) LIMITACIONES
1. Planificatorio: no se ejecutó ningún experimento; no se afirman resultados.
2. El workspace no contiene el repositorio de InfLLM: el mapeo de los niveles de diseño a parámetros reales del código (tamaño de unidad, m, k_r, método de resumen) debe verificarse al implementar; InfLLM oficial podría no exponer todas las granularidades (B2/B3 pueden requerir parches).
3. Familia de modelo primaria Llama-3; generalización a otras arquitecturas no probada (70B opcional).
4. LongBench no cubre 64K–128K; esas celdas dependen de benchmarks sintéticos (RULER/NIAH).
5. El desajuste de atención por paso (A1 atiende k_r·u ≪ K tokens) se mitiga solo parcialmente vía el análisis de sensibilidad compute-matched.
6. Se asume KV en FP16; la cuantización alteraría los presupuestos.
7. RULER/NIAH son sintéticos; LongBench aporta validez externa pero con documentos más cortos.

8) SUPUESTOS (separados de los requisitos fijos del brief)
- Cómputo: 4×A100/H100 80 GB, ~2 semanas; fallback 1 GPU.
- Modelo: LLaMA-3 8B primario; 70B opcional.
- InfLLM: v2 como sistema primario (nivel B4); unidades de v1 aproximadas por B1–B3.
- Tareas: RULER + NIAH + LongBench; 3 longitudes core (8K/32K/128K).
- El entorno de ejecución (no este workspace) dispondrá de red para descargar datasets y el repositorio de InfLLM.

PLAN FRAMEWORK (proposal only — no experiment run, no final design yet)

0) MATERIALS FOUND: /workspace contains only task.json (question + one-line track.md: "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."). No InfLLM code/docs/configs/datasets are inspectable. All InfLLM-internal details are marked UNCONFIRMED below and should be pinned via researcher clarification (budget 6) or the paper.

1) CORE QUESTION OPERATIONALIZATION
Decompose "how critical" into two factors with measurable effects:
- Factor A — dynamic context memory lookup: performance delta between InfLLM's dynamic retrieval and non-dynamic baselines, holding memory content and retrieval budget fixed.
- Factor B — unit representation: performance delta across alternative memory unit encodings, holding memory size budget and lookup fixed.
"Critical" is quantified as: (i) absolute effect size (accuracy/F1 points) of removing/changing each factor, (ii) interaction A×B, (iii) robustness across context length (e.g., 8K→1M) and information depth. A factor is "critical" if its removal causes a large, consistent drop (pre-registered threshold, e.g., ≥5 points average or ≥30% relative, to be set with researcher).
Design: 2 (lookup: dynamic vs fixed-baseline) × 2 (unit: native vs alternative) factorial, optionally +1 lookup variant (degraded/simplified lookup) as a dose-response arm.

2) LOOKUP AS INDEPENDENT VARIABLE
- A1 (full): InfLLM's native dynamic lookup (recursive retrieval over memory), UNCONFIRMED exact algorithm.
- A0 (off/fixed baseline): replace dynamic scoring with a position-independent fixed rule at the SAME retrieved-unit budget: e.g., recency window, uniform sampling, or top-k by static position. Use ≥2 fixed baselines to rule out "any retrieval works."
- A2 (degraded, optional): single-step retrieval instead of recursive, or noise-injected scores, to test sensitivity rather than binary on/off.
Critical control: same memory content, same number/size of retrieved units, same prompt assembly order, so the only difference is HOW units are selected.

3) UNIT REPRESENTATION
- U1: InfLLM's native unit (UNCONFIRMED — likely compressed KV/summary units; needs confirmation).
- U2: alternative at matched budget — e.g., raw token-level KV units, or larger fixed-length chunk summaries.
Match on: total memory capacity (units × size), total stored tokens, and information coverage (same source text compressed). If InfLLM's unit is itself a compressed representation, the key comparison is "native compression unit vs token-level vs chunk-level at equal memory budget."

4) LONG-CONTEXT TASKS & METRICS
Primary (retrieval-sensitive, isolates lookup):
- Needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH): 2–3 context lengths (e.g., 32K/128K/512K) × depths (10–90%), exact-match accuracy; report per-depth curves.
- Interference/multi-needle variant: one true + distractor needles (tests whether lookup, not just capacity, matters).
Secondary (downstream, generalization):
- Long-document QA (e.g., QuALITY or HotpotQA long contexts) — F1.
- Retrieval-augmented long-context summarization (e.g., PG-19) — ROUGE/length-controlled metric.
Metrics: task accuracy/F1 (primary); diagnostic retrieval hit-rate (was the right unit actually retrieved?); secondary efficiency: retrieved-token count, latency, memory footprint.
Pre-register primary metric = NIAH accuracy at the longest feasible context + QA F1; others for robustness.

5) CONTROLS
- Identical backbone, weights, fine-tuning/training procedure across all cells (lookup/unit ablations on the SAME trained model where possible; if unit changes require retraining, train matched variants with same data/optimizer/steps and report).
- Same memory content & capacity across unit conditions; same retrieval budget across lookup conditions; same prompt template, decoding (temp 0 or fixed seeds ×3), evaluation code.
- Balanced context lengths; needle position randomized and stratified; fixed random seeds; report variance across seeds.
- Sanity checks: (a) full-context oracle (no memory, full window) as upper bound; (b) no-memory lower bound; these bracket the contribution of the memory system as a whole.

6) CANDIDATE ANALYSIS PLAN
- Two-way ANOVA / mixed-effects regression (task, context length, depth as factors/covariates) on the factorial cells; report main effects, interaction, effect sizes (Cohen's d / Δpoints) with 95% CIs.
- Nonparametric fallback (permutation or Wilcoxon) if cell n is small.
- Multiplicity: pre-declare primary comparisons; Benjamini-Hochberg on secondary ones.
- Dose-response plots: accuracy vs context length and vs needle depth per condition; retrieval hit-rate vs accuracy correlation to link mechanism (lookup quality) to outcome.
- Decision rule: declare lookup "critical" if A0 drop ≥ pre-set threshold on ≥2 of 3 task families; same for unit choice; interaction reported separately.

7) FEASIBILITY BOUNDS & RESOURCE ASSUMPTIONS
- This workspace cannot run anything (no GPU, no network, no deps/datasets) — design only, as track.md states.
- Target environment assumptions (to confirm): 1×A100/H100 (80GB) per run is sufficient for 7–13B backbone at ≤128K; 512K–1M contexts need long-context-capable backbone or the InfLLM mechanism itself (chicken-and-egg: use 128K as the main ceiling, 512K as stretch).
- Runs: 2×2 factorial (+1 optional) × 3 tasks × 3 context lengths × 3 seeds ≈ 54–81 evaluation runs; NIAH-style synthetic data is cheap to generate; QA/summarization evals are the cost driver. Estimated order: ~5–15 GPU-days, not GPU-weeks.

payload.answer:
FINAL EXPERIMENT DESIGN (design-only deliverable; NO experiment was run or will be run in this workspace)

QUESTION: How critical are dynamic context memory lookup and the choice of unit representations to InfLLM's performance across long-context tasks?

0. STATUS AND SCOPE
- Deliverable: experiment design with rationale, controls, analysis plan, feasibility. No execution.
- Workspace evidence: /workspace contains only task.json; track.md = "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required." No InfLLM source, configs, or datasets are inspectable; network disabled.
- Labeling convention per final requirement: all InfLLM-internal mechanism details — (a) memory unit definition, (b) recursive retrieval algorithm, (c) whether fine-tuning is required — are uniformly marked 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】 wherever they appear. No claim is made about these internals beyond what is labeled.

1. RATIONALE
The question contains two ablatable components of InfLLM's memory-augmented architecture: (A) HOW memory units are selected at generation time (dynamic lookup) and (B) WHAT memory units are (unit representation). "Critical" is only meaningful relative to a counterfactual: performance when each component is removed or replaced while everything else is held fixed. A factorial design isolates main effects and their interaction, and evaluating across context lengths/depths distinguishes "helps everywhere" from "matters only at the edge of capacity." Bracketing conditions (full-context oracle, no-memory floor) separate the contribution of the memory system as a whole from the contribution of its sub-components.

2. CORE QUESTION OPERATIONALIZATION
- Factor A (lookup): ΔA = Perf(dynamic lookup) − Perf(fixed-baseline lookup), memory content and retrieval budget held identical.
- Factor B (units): ΔB = Perf(native unit) − Perf(alternative unit), lookup and memory budget held identical.
- Interaction: ΔA×B tests whether the choice of unit modulates the value of dynamic lookup.
- Pre-registered criticality rule (to confirm with researcher): a factor is "critical" if its removal/replacement causes a drop ≥5 accuracy points (or ≥30% relative) on the primary metric, averaged over context lengths, in at least 2 of 3 task families, with a 95% CI excluding zero.
- Moderators: context length (32K/128K/512K where feasible) and information depth (10–90%).

3. TREATMENT CONDITIONS
Factor A — dynamic context memory lookup (algorithm specifics 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】):
- A1 (dynamic): InfLLM's native dynamic lookup, used exactly as defined by the mechanism 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- A0 (fixed baseline): dynamic scoring replaced by a position-independent fixed rule with the SAME retrieved-unit budget. Two baselines for robustness: A0a = recency window; A0b = uniform sampling over memory.
- A2 (degraded, optional dose-response arm): simplified lookup (e.g., single retrieval pass instead of multi-pass/recursive 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】) or noise-perturbed scores.
Invariant across A conditions: identical memory content, identical number and size of retrieved units, identical prompt assembly position.

Factor B — unit representation (native unit definition 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】):
- B1 (native): InfLLM's native memory unit 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- B2 (alternative): a different unit at matched memory budget — e.g., raw token-level KV units or fixed-length chunk summaries, same source text, same total capacity (units × size) and same stored-token count as B1.
If B2 requires retraining while B1 uses the released weights (or vice versa), train matched variants with identical data, optimizer, and steps, and report training parity as a control check.

Factorial: A1×B1, A0a×B1, A0b×B1, A1×B2, A0a×B2 (A0b×B2 optional).
DEGRADED DESIGN (contingency): if lookup scoring is architecturally coupled to the native unit format 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】, A1×B2 is not realizable; then compare {A1×B1, A0×B1} and {A1×B2', A0×B2} where B2' uses the lookup compatible with B2, and state the A×B interaction as partially confounded.

4. TASKS AND METRICS
Primary (retrieval-sensitive; isolates lookup):
- T1 Needle-in-a-haystack: context lengths 32K/128K/512K × depths 10–90%; metric = exact-match accuracy; report per-depth curves.
- T2 Interference (multi-needle): one true needle + k distractor needles; tests whether selection (not just capacity) drives performance.
Secondary (downstream generalization):
- T3 Long-document multi-hop QA (e.g., QuALITY-style): F1.
- T4 Long-context summarization (e.g., PG-19): ROUGE-L / length-controlled score.
Pre-registered primary metrics: T1 accuracy at the longest feasible context, and T3 F1. T2/T4 for robustness.
Diagnostic: retrieval hit-rate (fraction of generations where the unit containing the answer was retrieved) — links mechanism to outcome.
Secondary efficiency: retrieved-token count, per-query latency, memory footprint.

5. CONTROLS
- Backbone and weights: identical across all cells; lookup ablations run on the SAME trained model. If unit change forces retraining, matched training procedure (same data, optimizer, steps, seeds). Whether the base mechanism itself requires fine-tuning is 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】 and must be resolved before execution.
- Memory parity: identical source text, identical capacity and stored-token budget across B conditions; identical retrieval budget across A conditions.
- Presentation: fixed prompt template, fixed unit insertion position, temperature 0 (or 3 fixed seeds for variance), identical evaluation code.
- Position control: needle/key position randomized and stratified across depths.
- Bracketing controls: (i) oracle = full context in window, no memory (upper bound); (ii) no-memory floor = generation without retrieved units (lower bound). These bound the memory system's total contribution.
- Random seeds: ≥3 for all primary comparisons; report per-seed results.
- Pre-registration: conditions, metrics, thresholds, and analysis code frozen before first run.

6. ANALYSIS PLAN
- Model: mixed-effects regression (random intercepts for seed and item/document) on the factorial cells; fixed effects: lookup, unit, lookup×unit, context length, depth. Report main effects, interaction, and effect sizes (Δpoints, Cohen's d) with 95% CIs.
- Fallback: permutation/Wilcoxon tests if cell n is small or normality fails.
- Multiplicity: primary comparisons (ΔA on T1, ΔB on T1, ΔA on T3) unadjusted; secondary comparisons Benjamini–Hochberg corrected.
- Dose-response: accuracy vs context length and vs depth per condition; Spearman correlation between retrieval hit-rate and task accuracy to test the causal chain lookup quality → retrieval → performance.
- Decision rule: apply the pre-registered criticality rule per factor; report interaction separately; a null on a factor is reported as evidence of non-criticality only if power (cell n, seed variance) supports it.

7. FEASIBILITY BOUNDS AND RESOURCE ASSUMPTIONS
- This workspace: cannot execute (no GPU, no network, no deps/datasets) — consistent with track.md; all execution statements below concern a hypothetical target environment 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Compute (assumed, to confirm): 1×A100/H100 (80GB) per run for a 7–13B backbone up to 128K; 512K is a stretch goal requiring a long-context-capable backbone or the memory mechanism itself (circularity noted; 128K is the hard main ceiling).
- Scale: 5 cells × 4 tasks × 3 context lengths × 3 seeds ≈ 180 evaluations; T1/T2 synthetic data are cheap to generate; T3/T4 are the cost driver. Order of magnitude: ~5–15 GPU-days.
- Staged execution: (i) pilot — T1 only, 8K–32K, 1 seed (~1 GPU-day) to validate harness and ablation code; (ii) full factorial at 32K/128K; (iii) 512K stretch if pilot passes.
- Kill criteria: abort full run if pilot shows any ablation cell is unimplementable (e.g., coupling discovered) or baseline variance exceeds 10 points across seeds.

8. KEY ASSUMPTIONS (mine, flagged)
- InfLLM = recursive-retrieval memory-augmented extension (Liu et al., 2024) — assumption.
- Lookup and unit are separable; else degraded design (Section 3).
- 7–13B open backbone can host the mechanism; 80GB GPU suffices to 128K.
- Pre-registered threshold (≥5 points / ≥30% relative) is acceptable.

9. UNCONFIRMED ITEMS (must remain open; uniformly labeled)
- Memory unit definition — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Recursive retrieval algorithm — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Whether fine-tuning is required, and with what data — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Official backbone(s) and context-length ceilings — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Architectural coupling between lookup and unit format — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
- Target execution environment (GPU, datasets, dependencies) — 【未确认 UNCONFIRMED】.
Suggested researcher confirmations (within 6-question budget): (1) confirm InfLLM variant and pin unit/lookup definitions; (2) fine-tuning requirement and data; (3) backbone and max context for the target environment.

payload.answer:
## 1) Repository / input inspection

The workspace is effectively empty. `/workspace` contains exactly **one file: `task.json`**. There is **no InfLLM source code, no configuration files, no task definitions, no dataset manifests, no README, and no benchmark lists** anywhere in the workspace (verified by recursive `find` for `.py/.yaml/.json/.md/.txt/.toml` and for `*infllm*`/`track.md` across the filesystem).

`task.json` holds only:
- the question (dynamic context memory lookup + unit representations → InfLLM long-context performance),
- a one-line `context` ("Design an experiment… do not claim an experiment was run"),
- a `documents.track.md` field whose value is just the stub: **"Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."**

So there is **no track.md file on disk** and **no project material to ground config/benchmark details**. The design must therefore rest on (a) the question itself and (b) well-established public knowledge of InfLLM (arXiv:2504.07610 — a method that decouples the pretrain context window from total sequence length via a fixed-size **dynamic context memory** that stores prior content as **units** and **retrieves/looks up** relevant content at generation time). I will flag every place the source is silent and the design hinges on a choice you should validate (see §3).

## 2) Proposed approach (skeleton)

This is a **2-factor ablation** on a fixed base LLM, using InfLLM as the "full" reference system.

**(a) Factors and isolation**
- **Factor A — Dynamic context memory lookup** (binary): **ON** (retrieve relevant memory during generation) vs **OFF** (no retrieval step). OFF is implemented as the cleanest single-variable change the code allows while keeping the *same total content available*; where memory and lookup are entangled, we define OFF as "attend over the sliding window only / no cross-window lookup" and state that explicitly.
- **Factor B — Unit representation** (categorical): the set of unit granularities InfLLM supports (assumed at minimum **token-level** vs **embedding-level** units; possibly chunk/segment level — to validate).
- **Isolation:** identical base model, data, eval protocol, and seed set across all cells; only the targeted factor changes. Report peak memory + latency per cell so efficiency trade-offs are visible (the whole point of InfLLM).

**(b) Task families** (chosen to stress different skills, each over a **range of sequence lengths** spanning the pretrain window up to very long / "infinite" contexts, e.g. 8K → 128K → 1M):
1. **Needle-in-a-haystack / needle-in-needle** → does lookup find sparse, single-fact info; length×depth heatmap.
2. **Multi-document QA** → integrating info scattered across a long context.
3. **Long-document summarization** → holistic understanding/generation over long spans.
(Optionally a 4th: retrieval-augmented / streaming generation, if InfLLM targets it.)

**(c) Metrics & baselines**
- **Quality:** accuracy / F1 (QA), ROUGE (summarization), recall@k (retrieval), NIAH success rate.
- **Efficiency + scaling:** peak memory, latency/throughput per token, and performance-vs-length curves (where each config degrades).
- **Baselines:** full InfLLM (reference); vanilla long-context LLM with full attention (accuracy upper bound, infeasible memory at long length); sliding/fixed window without memory (degenerate); plain RAG (retrieve top-k chunks, no persistent memory — isolates "retrieval" from "persistent memory").

**(d) Making individual + joint contributions readable**
Use a **2 × K factorial** (A ∈ {ON, OFF} × B ∈ {unit₁…unit_K}), with the full-model cell as the anchor. Then read:
- **Main effect of A** (lookup ON vs OFF, averaged over units) → how much dynamic lookup contributes.
- **Main effect of B** (unit choice, averaged over lookup) → how much representation choice contributes.
- **A×B interaction** → whether lookup's benefit depends on the unit representation (the *joint* contribution).
- **Per-cell Δ vs full model** → a contribution-decomposition table showing worst-case degradation (lookup OFF + weakest unit).

## 3) Consequential assumptions & uncertainties (validate before full design)

1. **Toggle interface for memory lookup.** I assume InfLLM exposes a config flag/module to disable lookup *without retraining*. If lookup is baked into the attention kernel, "OFF" may require a modified kernel — the single biggest design hinge. **Please validate.**
2. **Candidate unit representations.** I assume ≥ {token-level, embedding-level} units. The exact supported set, and how units are stored/quantized, is not in the workspace. **Please validate which units to include in Factor B.**
3. **Benchmark list.** I assume NIAH/needle-in-needle, multi-doc QA, and long-document summarization (InfLLM's typical long-context suite). Exact benchmarks InfLLM was actually evaluated on should be confirmed. **Please validate.**
4. **Sequence-length range.** Assume a pretrain window (~8K–32K) and evaluation up to ~100K–1M tokens; exact max length to confirm.
5. **Base model(s).** InfLLM is model-agnostic; which pretrained LLM(s) to run the ablation on (and at what size, given no-GPU/224-CPU environment) needs pinning.
6. **Cleanliness of the "OFF" ablation.** Whether memory and lookup are separable in code determines whether A is a true single-factor toggle or a coupled change.
7. **Compute reality.** Environment is CPU-only, no GPU, network disabled, no datasets. This is a **design-only** deliverable (per track.md); efficiency is treated as a *reported metric / feasibility constraint*, not something we can execute here. No results are claimed.

**Decision I need from you before the full protocol:** confirm (1) the lookup-toggle mechanism, (2) the exact unit-representation set for Factor B, and (3) the benchmark list + length range. With those three, the factorial cells, metric table, and baseline matrix can be written concretely.

The overall 2×K factorial structure, task family selection, baseline matrix, and contribution-decomposition table are sound and I'm ready for you to write the full design. Before you do, incorporate the following refinements into the complete protocol: 1. **Refine Factor A to three levels.** Your current binary ON/OFF conflates 'the memory buffer exists but retrieval is naive' with 'no memory mechanism at all.' To specifically isolate how critical the *dynamic* aspect of lookup is, use: (A1) full dynamic context-memory lookup (the InfLLM default); (A2) static/naive retrieval — memory buffer exists but the retrieval strategy is replaced by a simple rule (e.g., always attend to the most recent K units, or uniform attention over all stored units); (A3) no memory / sliding-window only. This 3-level factor lets you separate 'having a persistent memory' from 'having a smart lookup over it,' which is a more precise answer to the question. # Experiment Design: How Critical Are Dynamic Context-Memory Lookup and Unit Representation to InfLLM's Long-Context Performance?

**Status:** Design-only. No experiment has been executed; no benchmark numbers are reported. Every InfLLM-specific detail is either (P) grounded in public documentation (InfLLM, arXiv:2504.07610) or (A) a design assumption to be validated against the codebase before execution.

---

## 0. Repository / input state (basis for the design)
`/workspace` contains only `task.json` (question + one-line `track.md` stub: "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."). There is **no InfLLM source, config, dataset manifest, or benchmark list on disk**. The design therefore rests on the question's two named factors and public knowledge of InfLLM: a method that decouples the pretrain context window from total sequence length by keeping a fixed-size **dynamic context memory** that stores prior content as **units** and **retrieves/looks up** relevant content at generation time (P).

---

## 1. Research question and hypotheses
- **RQ:** How much of InfLLM's long-context performance is attributable to (A) the *dynamic context-memory lookup* mechanism and (B) the *choice of unit representation*, individually and jointly?
- **H_A:** Dynamic lookup (A1) beats naive retrieval (A2) and no-memory sliding window (A3); the gap A1−A3 measures "persistent memory + smart lookup," A1−A2 measures the *dynamic* lookup specifically, and A2−A3 measures the *persistent memory* specifically.
- **H_B:** Unit representation materially changes accuracy/efficiency on long-context tasks.
- **H_int:** The benefit of dynamic lookup (A1 vs A2/A3) depends on the unit representation (A×B interaction).

---

## 2. Factors and design

### Factor A — Context-memory lookup (3 levels)
- **A1 — Full dynamic context-memory lookup** (InfLLM default). Persistent memory + dynamic retrieval of relevant units at generation (P).
- **A2 — Static/naive retrieval.** The persistent memory buffer is kept, but the retrieval strategy is replaced by a simple, content-agnostic rule: e.g. (a) most-recent-K units, or (b) uniform attention over all stored units. This isolates the *dynamic* aspect of lookup from the mere *existence* of a persistent memory.
- **A3 — No memory / sliding-window only.** No persistent buffer; the model attends only over a fixed sliding window. This is the degenerate "no long-context mechanism" cell.

**Feasibility caveat (must be validated, assumption A):** If the InfLLM codebase bakes lookup into the attention kernel such that the retrieval strategy cannot be swapped without retraining, then **A2 is infeasible**. In that case fall back to the **binary** design {A1, A3} and explicitly record the limitation: we can then measure "memory+lookup vs none" but *cannot* separate the *dynamic* component of lookup from the persistent-memory component. The code-level validation in §7 is what decides which of {3-level, 2-level} is realized.

### Factor B — Unit representation (K levels)
The set of unit granularities InfLLM supports (assumption A; to be enumerated from the code). Minimum viable set:
- **B1 — token-level units** (raw token IDs / text chunks).
- **B2 — embedding-level units** (continuous representations).
- **B3 — chunk/segment units** (coarser grouping), *if supported*.
Design is written for K ∈ {2, 3}; cell counts below are given for both.

### Factorization
**3 (A) × K (B) factorial**, with the full InfLLM configuration (A1 + the InfLLM-default unit) as the anchor/reference cell. This decomposition makes individual and joint contributions directly readable:
- **Main effect A** = mean over B of (A1 vs A2 vs A3) → importance of the lookup mechanism, split into "memory" (A2−A3) and "dynamic" (A1−A2) components.
- **Main effect B** = mean over A of unit levels → importance of representation choice.
- **A×B interaction** → whether lookup's benefit is representation-dependent (the joint contribution).

### Task families (3), each over a range of sequence lengths
Chosen to stress distinct skills; each run at multiple lengths spanning the pretrain window up to very long contexts (assumption A on exact max length):
1. **Needle-in-a-haystack / needle-in-needle** — sparse single-fact retrieval; reported as length×depth success heatmap. Most sensitive to whether lookup can *find* a unit.
2. **Multi-document QA** — integrating information scattered across a long context (accuracy/F1).
3. **Long-document summarization** — holistic understanding/generation over long spans (ROUGE).
*(Optional 4th: retrieval-augmented / streaming generation, only if InfLLM targets it — assumption A.)*

**Sequence-length ladder (assumption A, to validate max):** e.g. 8K → 32K → 128K → (256K/1M if supported). The 8K/32K points sit at/just beyond the pretrain window; the long points test the "infinite-length" claim.

### Baselines (external, for context)
- **Full InfLLM** (reference anchor).
- **Vanilla long-context LLM, full attention** — accuracy upper bound; infeasible memory at long length (shows what "perfect recall" would look like).
- **Sliding/fixed window without memory** — overlaps A3; included to show the ablation is on the same footing as a real baseline.
- **Plain RAG** (retrieve top-k chunks, no persistent memory) — isolates "retrieval" from "persistent memory," i.e., a retrieval-without-memory contrast.

---

## 3. Metrics (per cell)
- **Quality:** accuracy / F1 (QA), ROUGE (summarization), recall@k (retrieval), NIAH success rate (length×depth heatmap).
- **Efficiency (first-class, since InfLLM's purpose is long-context efficiency):** peak GPU memory, decode latency / tokens-per-second, total tokens processed.
- **Length scaling:** performance-vs-length curve per cell (where and how fast each config degrades).
- **Headline deliverables (kept per request):**
  1. **Per-cell Δ vs. full-model table** (each ablation cell's quality and efficiency delta vs. the A1+default-unit anchor) — the most readable contribution decomposition.
  2. **Performance-vs-length scaling curves** per (A,B) configuration.

---

## 4. Statistical analysis plan
- **(a) Model.** Linear mixed-effects model per task-family metric:
  `score ~ A * B + (1 | task) + (1 | sequence_length)`, with A and B as fixed factors and task + sequence length as crossed random effects (random intercepts). For paired/deterministic metrics we also report **paired comparisons** (same examples, same seeds across cells) as a robustness check. Report fixed-effect estimates with 95% CIs.
- **(b) Multiple comparisons.** The factorial yields many pairwise contrasts; control family-wise error with **Bonferroni** (simple, conservative, appropriate given the small number of pre-registered contrasts of interest) or **Benjamini–Hochberg FDR** (less conservative, preferred if we explore many cells). Pre-register which contrasts are *primary* (A1−A2, A2−A3, A1−A3, B1−B2, interaction) and apply the chosen correction across the full contrast set.
- **(c) Power / sample size (rough planning estimate, not a measurement).** For a paired/mixed design to detect a moderate effect (Cohen's d ≈ 0.3–0.5) at α=0.05, power 0.8: **≥ ~30–50 examples per (task, length) cell** and **≥ 3 independent runs** (3 random seeds for stochastic decoding, or 1 fixed seed + ≥ 3 sampled decodes) to estimate within-cell variance. This is a rough lower bound; a formal power analysis should be run once a pilot gives the true within-cell SD.
- **(d) Interaction reporting.** Report the **A×B interaction contrast** plus **simple main effects of A at each unit level** (i.e., A1−A2−A3 profile separately for B1, B2, [B3]). A significant interaction ⇒ the value of dynamic lookup is representation-dependent; we then interpret A's effect *conditional on* B rather than averaging.

---

## 5. Feasibility and minimum-viable experiment (design-only; CPU-only, no GPU, no network, no datasets available here)

### (a) Compute estimate (planning magnitude only — not a measurement)
Full factorial: **3 (A) × K (B) × 3 (tasks) × 4 (lengths)** cells.
- K=2 → **72 cells**; K=3 → **108 cells**. Each cell = long-context decoding over the length ladder (up to 1M tokens at the top), which is the dominant cost.
- Order-of-magnitude planning estimate: on the order of **10²–10³ GPU-hours** for the full factorial (driven by the long-length, long-context decode cells), scaling with K and with how many examples/seeds per cell. The long-length cells are disproportionately expensive; capping the top length or reducing examples is the main cost lever. *(Clearly a planning estimate to refine after the code-level validations in §7.)*

### (b) Minimum viable experiment (MVE)
**1 task × 2 sequence lengths × 2 unit types × 3 lookup levels = 12 cells** (or 6 cells if A2 is infeasible → binary A).
- Chosen task: **needle-in-a-haystack** (most sensitive to the lookup mechanism, cheapest to score).
- Lengths: one at/just beyond the pretrain window (e.g. 32K) and one long (e.g. 128K).
- Units: token vs embedding.
This 12-cell MVE still separates "persistent memory" (A2−A3), "dynamic lookup" (A1−A2), and "representation choice" (B1−B2) at reduced precision — enough to answer the RQ directionally before committing to the full factorial.

### (c) Code-level validations that MUST precede execution
1. **Confirm the lookup-toggle interface exists** and can be set to A2 (swap retrieval strategy) and A3 (disable memory) *without retraining*. This decides 3-level vs binary Factor A — the single biggest design hinge.
2. **Enumerate the supported unit representations** and fix K (token / embedding / chunk) — defines Factor B.
3. **Confirm maximum supported sequence length** and set the length ladder accordingly.
4. **Confirm the base model(s) the codebase supports** and pin the default (see §6).
5. **Verify memory and lookup are separable** so A is a clean single-factor ablation (else document the coupling).
6. **Confirm eval harness / metric availability** for the three task families (or substitute equivalent public long-context benchmarks).

---

## 6. Base model (design assumption, subject to codebase support)
**Default: LLaMA-3-8B.** One-line justification: a widely available, well-known 7–8B decoder that fits the "apply InfLLM on a strong pretrained LLM" framing and is a reasonable size for long-context ablations without prohibitive cost. *(Assumption A: InfLLM is model-agnostic; the actual supported base(s) must be confirmed via the §7 validations, and the default may be swapped to whatever the codebase natively supports.)*

---

## 7. Threats to validity
- **Task-difficulty confounds:** the three task families probe different skills; a factor that looks "critical" on needle-in-a-haystack may not be on summarization. Mitigated by treating *task* as a random effect and reporting per-family effects rather than pooling only.
- **Finite-sample variance at very long contexts:** long-context examples are expensive and few, so the top-length cells have high variance and weak power. Mitigated by the random effect for sequence length, ≥3 runs, and by flagging top-length results as lower-confidence.
- **Pre-existing long-context capability of the base model:** if the base LLM already handles some long contexts natively, A3 (sliding window) may understate the true need for memory, muddying the "how critical is memory" estimate. Mitigated by including the vanilla full-attention baseline as an upper bound and choosing lengths that exceed the base window.
- **A2 feasibility / coupling:** if A2 is infeasible or lookup is entangled with the attention path, the "dynamic" component of lookup cannot be cleanly isolated (fallback to binary A is documented).
- **Efficiency–quality trade-off masking:** a factor may trade accuracy for memory/latency; reporting both prevents a misleading "quality-only" conclusion.
- **Benchmark selection:** the exact InfLLM benchmark set is not in the workspace (assumption A); using substitute public benchmarks could shift absolute results (though not the relative ablation, which is the target of the RQ).

---

## 8. Deliverables (readability-first)
1. **Per-cell Δ vs. full-model table** (quality + efficiency deltas for every A×B cell).
2. **Performance-vs-length scaling curves** per configuration.
3. **Contribution-decomposition:** memory component (A2−A3), dynamic-lookup component (A1−A2), representation component (B main effect), and joint (A×B) — each with CIs and corrected significance.
4. **MVE report** (12-cell) as a go/no-go gate before the full factorial.

All other specifics (lookup-toggle interface, exact unit set, max sequence length, supported base model, benchmark list, compute magnitude) are explicitly marked as design assumptions (A) with a mandatory pre-execution code-level validation step (§7). ## 1. Workspace Inspection Report

**Files present in `/workspace/`:**
- `task.json` (434 bytes) — the only file. It contains the question, context, and a `documents` key with one entry `track.md` whose value is the string *"Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required."*
- No Python source files, no input data files, no sample word lists, no CSVs, no config, no test fixtures, no `requirements.txt`, no `pyproject.toml`.

**Python interpreter:**
- `python3` → **Python 3.14.4** (system Python at `/bin/python3`).
- No project dependencies preinstalled (per environment metadata). Standard library is available.

**Environment constraints:**
- Sandboxed via **bubblewrap**; **network disabled**; no GPU; 224 CPU affinity slots.
- **No datasets** are provided.

**Confirmation: there is no input data to sort.** The workspace contains zero data files. The program to be designed must accept its word list as a parameter (function argument or hard-coded list in the test harness); there is no file to read.

---

## 2. Proposed Experiment Design (Approach)

### 2.1 Framing
The "experiment" is a **deterministic test suite** that validates a reference implementation of the word-sorting function against a fixed battery of input→expected-output pairs. Because the task is design-only, the deliverable is the *specification of that suite* plus the *reference implementation logic*, not an executed run.

### 2.2 Reference Implementation (to be specified, not yet written)
```
def sort_words(words: list[str]) -> str:
    return " ".join(sorted(words, key=<COLLATION_KEY>))
```
- **Input contract:** a Python `list[str]` of words.
- **Output contract:** a single `str` — the sorted words joined by exactly one ASCII space (U+0020), no leading/trailing spaces, no embedded newlines.
- `<COLLATION_KEY>` is the single most consequential design decision (see §3, item 1). The default proposal is **plain codepoint order via `sorted(words)`** (i.e., `key=None`), which is the most common interpretation of "alphabetical" in a Python context. This is flagged as an open decision.

### 2.3 Test / Evaluation Structure

**A. Test-case table**

Each case is a tuple `(name, input_list, expected_output_string)`. The suite covers:

| # | Name | Input | What it pins down |
|---|------|-------|-------------------|
| 1 | `identity_single` | `["hello"]` | Single word → same word, no extra spaces |
| 2 | `identity_two` | `["b", "a"]` | Minimal swap; output `"a b"` |
| 3 | `already_sorted` | `["a", "b", "c"]` | Pre-sorted input is a no-op; output `"a b c"` |
| 4 | `reverse_sorted` | `["c", "b", "a"]` | Full reversal; output `"a b c"` |
| 5 | `duplicates` | `["banana", "apple", "banana", "apple"]` | Duplicates preserved (stable multiset); output `"apple apple banana banana"` |
| 6 | `case_mixed` | `["Banana", "apple", "Cherry", "apple"]` | Case-sensitivity behaviour (see §3 item 1) |
| 7 | `empty_list` | `[]` | Empty input → empty string `""` |
| 8 | `single_char_words` | `["z", "a", "m", "b"]` | Single characters; output `"a b m z"` |
| 9 | `numeric_words` | `["item10", "item2", "item1"]` | Lexicographic (not numeric) ordering: `"item1 item10 item2"` |
| 10 | `unicode_words` | `["café", "cafe", "CAFÉ"]` | Codepoint vs locale collation (see §3 item 1) |
| 11 | `long_list` | 100 pre-generated words | Performance sanity; output is one line |
| 12 | `words_with_hyphen` | `["well-known", "well", "known"]` | Hyphenated words treated as single tokens |

**B. Correctness checks (per test case)**

For each case the harness verifies **all** of the following:

1. **Permutation check (multiset equality):**
   `collections.Counter(actual_output.split(" ")) == collections.Counter(input_list)`
   This confirms no words are lost, added, or mangled.

2. **Sort-order check:**
   `actual_output.split(" ") == sorted(input_list, key=<COLLATION_KEY>)`
   This confirms the exact expected ordering under the chosen collation.

3. **Format check (single space-joined line):**
   - `actual_output == " ".join(actual_output.split(" "))` — no leading/trailing/double spaces.
   - `"\n" not in actual_output` — no embedded newlines.
   - `actual_output.count("  ") == 0` — no double-space (redundant but explicit).
   - Equivalently: `actual_output == " ".join(words)` where `words` is the sorted list.

4. **Type check:**
   `isinstance(actual_output, str)` — the return type is a string, not a list.

**C. Pass/fail criterion**
A test case passes only if checks 1–4 all hold. The suite passes if all 12 cases pass.

### 2.4 Controls

- **Positive control (Case 1):** a single word must round-trip unchanged. If this fails, the formatter is broken independent of sorting.
- **Neutral control (Case 3):** an already-sorted list must be returned in identical order. If this fails, the sort is not stable or the key function is inconsistent.
- **Negative control (Case 9):** numeric-looking words (`item2` vs `item10`) must sort lexicographically, not numerically. If the implementation accidentally converts to int, this case catches it.
- **Boundary control (Case 7):** empty list must yield `""` (empty string), not `" "` or `None`.
- **Locale control (Case 10):** makes the collation assumption explicit — under codepoint order, `"CAFÉ"` < `"cafe"` < `"café"`; under a locale-aware key the order would differ. This case is designed to *fail* if the key is changed without updating the expected output, forcing an intentional decision.

### 2.5 Feasibility
- Entirely standard-library (`collections`, `unittest` or plain `assert`). No third-party imports needed.
- Runs in < 1 s on any hardware. No network, no GPU, no data files.
- Compatible with Python 3.14.4 in the bubblewrap sandbox.

---

## 3. Consequential Assumptions & Uncertainties (Flagged for Decision)

The source task — *"alphabetically sorts a list of words and returns them as a single line of text with spaces between words"* — does **not** pin down the following. Each is flagged with the default I am proposing and the alternative:

| # | Decision point | Default proposal | Alternative(s) | Why it matters |
|---|---------------|-----------------|----------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Collation / "alphabetical" rule** | **Plain Unicode codepoint order** (Python `sorted()` with no key). Uppercase sorts before lowercase; accented chars sort by codepoint. | (a) Case-insensitive: `key=str.casefold`. (b) Locale-aware: `locale.strcoll` or `pycollate`. (c) Dictionary order ignoring punctuation. | Changes expected outputs for Cases 6 and 10. "Alphabetical" in everyday English often implies case-insensitive, but Python's default is codepoint. **This is the highest-impact open decision.** |
| 2 | **Duplicate handling** | **Preserve all duplicates** (stable sort; multiset is conserved). | Remove duplicates (return unique sorted words). | The phrase "sorts a list" implies a permutation (preservation). But if the intent is "sort a set of words," deduplication might be expected. Affects Case 5. |
| 3 | **Empty / whitespace-only input** | Empty list `[]` → return `""`. A list containing `""` or `"  "` → treat as a token and sort it among the others (codepoint: `""` and spaces sort before letters). | Filter out empty/whitespace-only tokens before sorting. | Affects Case 7 and any hypothetical case with `""` in the list. The task doesn't say the input is guaranteed non-empty or that tokens are non-empty. |
| 4 | **Input interface** | Function takes a `list[str]` parameter. | Accepts a raw string and splits on whitespace; reads from a file; reads from stdin. | The task says "a list of words," which most naturally maps to a Python list. But the I/O boundary is unspecified. This affects the harness shape but not the core logic. |
| 5 | **Trailing newline in output** | **No trailing newline.** The return value is `str` with no `\n`. | Allow / require a single trailing `\n` (conventional for "a line of text"). | "Single line of text" is ambiguous: a line in a file typically ends with `\n`, but a Python `str` representing a line does not need one. Affects the format check. |

# Experiment Design: Alphabetical Word-Sort Program

## 1. Objective & Scope

Design a deterministic test suite that validates a reference implementation of a function which takes a list of words, sorts them alphabetically, and returns them as a single space-joined line of text. The deliverable is this design specification. No code is executed as part of the design task.

## 2. Reference-Implementation Specification

**Signature:** `def sort_words(words: list[str]) -> str`

**Input contract:** A Python list of strings. Each element is one word (opaque token; no further tokenization). The list may be empty. Elements may contain any Unicode characters, including uppercase, lowercase, digits, hyphens, and accented letters.

**Output contract:** A single `str`. The sorted words joined by exactly one ASCII space (U+0020). No leading or trailing spaces. No embedded or trailing newline. Empty input yields `""`.

**Collation key:** Plain Unicode codepoint order — Python's default `sorted(words)` with no key function. Uppercase letters (U+0041–U+005A) sort before lowercase (U+0061–U+007A). Accented characters sort by their codepoint (e.g., `é` U+00E9 > `e` U+0065). This is the one-line implementation:

```
return " ".join(sorted(words))
```

*Alternatives not adopted (see §7):* case-insensitive (`key=str.casefold`), locale-aware (`locale.strcoll` / `pycollate`), dictionary-style (strip punctuation, ignore case).

## 3. Test-Case Table

All expected outputs below assume plain codepoint order.

| # | Name | Input | Expected output |
|---|------|-------|-----------------|
| 1 | `identity_single` | `["hello"]` | `"hello"` |
| 2 | `identity_two` | `["b", "a"]` | `"a b"` |
| 3 | `already_sorted` | `["a", "b", "c"]` | `"a b c"` |
| 4 | `reverse_sorted` | `["c", "b", "a"]` | `"a b c"` |
| 5 | `duplicates` | `["banana","apple","banana","apple"]` | `"apple apple banana banana"` |
| 6 | `case_mixed` | `["Banana","apple","Cherry","apple"]` | `"Banana Cherry apple apple"` |
| 7 | `empty_list` | `[]` | `""` |
| 8 | `single_char` | `["z","a","m","b"]` | `"a b m z"` |
| 9 | `numeric_words` | `["item10","item2","item1"]` | `"item1 item10 item2"` |
| 10 | `unicode_words` | `["café","cafe","CAFÉ"]` | `"CAFÉ cafe café"` |
| 11 | `long_list` | 100 distinct lowercase words (pre-generated, fixed seed) | `" ".join(sorted(words_100))` — one line, 99 single spaces |
| 12 | `hyphenated` | `["well-known","well","known"]` | `"known well well-known"` |

Case 6 rationale: `B`(66) < `C`(67) < `a`(97), so both uppercase words precede both lowercase ones.
Case 9 rationale: lexicographic, not numeric — `"item1"` < `"item10"` < `"item2"` because `1` < `2` at position 5.
Case 10 rationale: `C`(67) < `c`(99); within lowercase, `e`(101) < `é`(233).
Case 12 rationale: `"well"` is a prefix of `"well-known"`, so the shorter string sorts first.

## 4. Correctness Checks (Analysis Plan)

For every test case, all four checks must pass:

1. **Multiset (permutation) check**
   `Counter(actual.split(" ")) == Counter(input_list)`
   No words lost, added, or altered.

2. **Sort-order check**
   `actual.split(" ") == sorted(input_list)`
   Exact expected sequence under codepoint collation.

3. **Format check**
   `actual == " ".join(actual.split(" "))` and `"\n" not in actual`
   Confirms single-space joining, no leading/trailing/double spaces, no newlines.

4. **Type check**
   `isinstance(actual, str)`
   Return value is a string, not a list or None.

A test case passes iff checks 1–4 all hold. The suite passes iff all 12 cases pass.

## 5. Controls

| Control | Case # | Guards against |
|---------|--------|----------------|
| Positive (round-trip) | 1 | Formatter bug that adds/removes spaces even for trivial input |
| Neutral (no-op) | 3 | Unstable sort or inconsistent key that reorders already-sorted data |
| Negative (lexicographic trap) | 9 | Accidental numeric parsing of word content |
| Boundary (empty) | 7 | Off-by-one in join, `None` return, or `" "` instead of `""` |
| Locale (codepoint vs locale) | 10 | Implicit locale or case-folding that would silently change order; forces an explicit collation decision |

## 6. Feasibility & Resources

- **Dependencies:** Python standard library only (`collections.Counter`, `sorted`). No third-party packages.
- **Runtime:** 12 cases, all ≤ 100 elements. Expected wall-clock < 1 s on any hardware.
- **Environment:** Runs inside the existing bubblewrap sandbox (Python 3.14.4, network disabled, no GPU required). No data files, no network calls, no GPU.
- **Reproducibility:** Case 11 uses a fixed-seed generator; all other inputs are literal. The suite is fully deterministic.

## 7. Assumptions & Limitations

Six decisions are not pinned down by the source task. The chosen default and the one-line alternative for each:

| # | Decision | Chosen default | Alternative |
|---|----------|---------------|-------------|
| 1 | Collation rule | Plain codepoint order (`sorted(words)`) | Case-insensitive: `key=str.casefold`; or locale-aware: `locale.strcoll` |
| 2 | Duplicates | Preserved (stable sort; multiset conserved) | Deduplicate: `sorted(set(words))` |
| 3 | Empty / whitespace-only tokens | Treated as valid tokens, sorted in place | Filtered out before sorting |
| 4 | Input interface | Function parameter: `list[str]` | Raw string split on whitespace; or file/stdin |
| 5 | Trailing newline | None — return value is the bare string | Append `"\n"` to make a conventional text line |
| 6 | Word boundary | Each list element is one opaque word | Input is a raw string requiring tokenization / punctuation stripping |

All six defaults compose to the minimal, most literal reading of the spec. Changing any one requires updating only the expected-output strings for the affected cases (primarily 6, 7, 10) — the harness structure and checks are unaffected.

# Experiment Design: Verification of a Word-Sorting Program

**Status:** Design-only deliverable. No experiment has been executed; no runtime results are claimed. This document is self-contained so an implementer can build the SUT and run the battery without further questions.

---

## 1. Objective and Scope

**Objective:** Verify that a word-sorting program (the System Under Test, SUT) (a) sorts a given list of words in *alphabetical* order and (b) returns the result as a *single line of text* with a single space between consecutive words.

**In scope:**
- Correctness of sort order (total ordering of the input words).
- Correctness of output formatting (single line, single-space separators, no extra whitespace).
- Behavior on edge cases (empty, single, duplicates, digits/special chars, mixed case, diacritics, large inputs, already-sorted/reverse inputs).

**Out of scope:**
- Performance/throughput at production scale (only a bounded large-input case for stability).
- Input parsing from files/CLI/network (the contract is in-memory list in → string out).
- Natural-language "word segmentation" of a raw string (input is already a list of words).

**Definition of "alphabetical" (baseline, per approved approach):** deterministic, case-sensitive, lexicographic ordering by Unicode code points (Python `str` default ordering). Alternatives are documented as variants in §10.

---

## 2. System Under Test — Language-Agnostic I/O Contract

```
function sort_words(words: list[str]) -> str
```

**Preconditions / input contract:**
- `words` is a list (sequence) of strings.
- Each element is treated as an opaque "word" (any characters allowed; no internal splitting).
- The function must not mutate the input list.
- The function must be deterministic: same input → same output, every run (no locale, no randomness, no time dependence).

**Output contract (canonical form):**
- Returns a single string on one line (no `\n`, `\r`, or other line breaks).
- Words appear in sorted (code-point) order.
- Consecutive words are separated by exactly **one** ASCII space (`U+0020`).
- **No** leading space, **no** trailing space.
- Empty input list → returns the empty string `""` (not a single space).

**Language-agnostic note:** The contract is defined in abstract terms; the reference implementation and test harness are written in Python 3 (available in the runtime) for concreteness. A SUT in any language satisfies the contract if it meets the input/output rules above.

---

## 3. Oracle and Reference Implementation

**Independent oracle (Python 3):**

```python
def oracle_sort_words(words):
    # code-point, case-sensitive sort + single-space join, no trailing ws
    return " ".join(sorted(words))
```

- `sorted()` uses Unicode code-point comparison for `str` — exactly the baseline definition in §1.
- `" ".join(...)` guarantees single-space separators and no leading/trailing whitespace; `join([])` yields `""`.

**Role of the oracle:** It is the *reference*, not the SUT. The SUT is an independent implementation; the oracle provides the expected output for each case. Because the oracle is trivial and obviously correct, discrepancies localize to the SUT.

**Two-tier checking (see §5):**
- Tier A (specification): hardcoded expected strings, independent of the oracle (guards against a shared mis-specification).
- Tier B (property-based): `sut(words) == oracle_sort_words(words)` across generated inputs.

---

## 4. Test Battery — Full Case Table

All "expected" strings below are the canonical single-line outputs. `|` marks string boundaries for readability only (not part of the string).

| # | Category | Input list | Expected output (single line) |
|---|----------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | Empty | `[]` | `` (empty string) |
| 2 | Single word | `["hello"]` | `hello` |
| 3 | Basic, distinct | `["banana","apple","cherry"]` | `apple banana cherry` |
| 4 | Duplicates | `["banana","apple","banana"]` | `apple banana banana` |
| 5 | Mixed case | `["Banana","apple","Banana"]` | `Banana Banana apple` |
| 6 | Digits / special chars | `["a1","-x","_y","a"]` | `-x _y a a1` |
| 7 | Punctuation ordering | `["!","a","A"]` | `! A a` |
| 8 | Diacritics (code point) | `["cafe","café","b"]` | `b cafe café` |
| 9 | Already sorted | `["a","b","c","d"]` | `a b c d` |
| 10 | Reverse sorted | `["d","c","b","a"]` | `a b c d` |
| 11 | Two words | `["b","a"]` | `a b` |
| 12 | Numeric-looking strings lex | `["10","2","1"]` | `1 10 2` |
| 13 | Prefix relationship | `["a","ab","abc"]` | `a ab abc` |
| 14 | Trailing-space rejection | `["  x","y"]` (word with leading space) | `  x y` (word preserved verbatim; only *separators* are canonical) |
| 15 | Large input (stability) | 10,000 distinct words, e.g. `["w%05d" % i for i in range(10000)]` | `" ".join(sorted(...))` — verified by property check, not by hand |

**Ordering rationale for non-obvious rows (code points):**
- Row 5: `B`(U+0042) < `a`(U+0061), so both `Banana` precede `apple`; the two `Banana` are equal and stable.
- Row 6: `-`(U+002D) < `_`(U+005F) < `a`(U+0061); `a` is a prefix of `a1` so `a` < `a1`.
- Row 7: `!`(U+0021) < `A`(U+0041) < `a`(U+0061).
- Row 8: `b` first; `cafe` vs `café` differ at last code point `e`(U+0065) < `é`(U+00E9), so `cafe` < `café`.
- Row 12: lexicographic, not numeric: `1` < `10` < `2`.
- Row 14: clarifies that the SUT sorts/preserves words **verbatim** and only controls the *separators*; internal/edge whitespace inside a word is not stripped (documented behavioral choice).

---

## 5. Controls

**A. Hardcoded controls (Tier A):** Rows 1–14 are assertions of *exact* expected strings independently specified (not computed by the oracle at authoring time). They protect against a shared bug in SUT and oracle agreeing on a wrong answer.

**B. Property-based control (Tier B):** For a set of generated inputs, assert the invariant:
```
sut(words) == " ".join(sorted(words))
```
Generated families:
- Random multisets of 0–50 words drawn from an alphabet including lowercase, uppercase, digits, `- _ !`, and `é`.
- Shuffled versions of a fixed 10,000-word list (order-invariance check: output depends only on the multiset, not input order).
- Idempotence: `sut(sut_output_as_single_token_list)` is consistent — i.e., re-sorting the output tokens reproduces the same output.
- Format invariants on every output: `output == " ".join(output.split(" "))` (no double/leading/trailing spaces) and `"\n" not in output and "\r" not in output`.

**C. Negative controls:** Deliberately wrong reference behaviors that the battery must *reject*, to confirm the assertions are sensitive:
- A sort that is case-insensitive (should FAIL row 5 under the baseline).
- A formatter that appends a trailing space (should FAIL all non-empty rows).
- A formatter that uses two-space separators (should FAIL).
These confirm the test harness is not vacuously passing.

---

## 6. Assertion and Success Criteria

- **Per-case assertion:** `sut(words) == expected` (strict string equality against the canonical expected string in §4, Tier A).
- **Property assertion:** `sut(words) == oracle_sort_words(words)` plus the format invariants in §5B (Tier B).
- **Success criterion (PASS):** The SUT passes **100%** of Tier A rows (1–14), **all** Tier B generated cases, and all format invariants, with **zero** trailing/leading/double-space or line-break violations.
- **FAIL:** Any single mismatch. Whitespace variations (trailing space, extra spaces, line breaks) are **not** tolerated — strict equality only.

---

## 7. Analysis Plan

**Per-case result:** `PASS` / `FAIL`, with the diff (input, expected, actual) recorded for each FAIL.

**Failure classification taxonomy** (each FAIL is tagged to localize the defect):
1. **Sort-order error** — right words, wrong relative order. Sub-tags:
   - `case-handling` (e.g., case-insensitive vs required case-sensitive) — indicates §10 variant confusion.
   - `codepoint-vs-locale` (e.g., diacritic ordering) — row 8.
   - `numeric-assumption` (lexicographic vs numeric) — row 12.
   - `prefix/stability` (equal or prefix keys) — rows 4, 13.
2. **Formatting error** — order correct, separators/whitespace wrong:
   - `trailing-space`, `leading-space`, `multi-space`, `line-break`, `empty-input-not-empty-string` (row 1).
3. **Contract violation** — input mutated, nondeterminism across runs, or wrong type returned.
4. **Crash/exception** — SUT raised on an input (e.g., row 15 large input, row 14).

**Coverage report over edge categories:** For each category in §4 (empty, single, duplicates, mixed-case, digits/special, punctuation, diacritics, sorted, reverse, prefix, large) report cases-run / cases-passed. A category is "covered" only if at least one dedicated case exists and passes.

**Aggregate verdict:** SUT is verified iff all categories are covered and pass, Tier B holds, and no negative control (§5C) accidentally passes (i.e., the harness detects the injected defects).

---

## 8. Rationale for Each Design Choice

- **Why case-sensitive code-point sort (baseline):** It is deterministic, locale-independent, and reproducible across machines/CI without environment configuration. Real-world "alphabetical" is ambiguous (case, accents, collation); pinning to code points makes the contract unambiguous and testable. Case-insensitive and locale-aware are real alternatives, so they are preserved as documented variants (§10) rather than silently chosen — this keeps the design honest about the ambiguity.
- **Why strict string equality:** The task specifies a precise output shape ("single line ... spaces between words"). Strict equality on the canonical form makes success binary and unambiguous, and it directly catches the most likely real defects (trailing space, double space, line breaks). Allowing whitespace variants would weaken the verification and hide formatting bugs.
- **Why these edge cases:** Each row targets a distinct, commonly-wrong behavior:
  - Empty/single → boundary handling and the `""`-not-`" "` contract.
  - Duplicates & prefix → stability and prefix ordering.
  - Digits/special/punctuation → lexicographic (not numeric) and code-point ordering of non-letters.
  - Mixed case → the central "what is alphabetical?" decision.
  - Diacritics → code-point vs collation distinction.
  - Sorted/reverse → order-invariance and no accidental re-sort assumptions.
  - Large input → stability/complexity sanity (O(n log n), no timeout) without implying a performance benchmark.
- **Why an independent oracle + hardcoded controls:** A single source of expected values risks a shared bug. Hardcoded Tier A strings are specified by hand; the oracle is used for Tier B generation. The two tiers cross-validate each other.
- **Why negative controls:** To prove the harness actually discriminates (not vacuously passing) by confirming it rejects deliberately broken behaviors.

---

## 9. Feasibility Assessment

- **Resources:** Pure in-memory computation on system Python 3.14.4 (confirmed available). No GPU, no network, no preinstalled third-party dependencies required (only the standard library: `sorted`, `join`, optionally `random` for generation).
- **Runtime:** Rows 1–14 are O(small) and run in microseconds. Row 15 (10k words) is O(n log n) ≈ microseconds-to-low-milliseconds. The full battery, including Tier B generation (hundreds of cases), completes well under a second. Runtime budget is effectively non-binding.
- **Dependencies:** None beyond the Python standard library. Fully offline-compatible (network disabled is fine).
- **Reproducibility:** Deterministic by design — fixed seed for any random generation, fixed expected strings, locale-independent code-point ordering. Same inputs always produce the same verdict; results are reproducible on any Python 3 environment.
- **Effort:** The SUT is a ~1-line function in any language; the harness is a small table-driven script. Low implementation and maintenance cost.

**Verdict:** Highly feasible as a design-only verification; all checks are cheap, deterministic, and dependency-free.

---

## 10. Limitations and Documented Variants

**Limitations:**
- The baseline pins "alphabetical" to code-point, case-sensitive ordering. If stakeholders actually intend linguistic/collation order, the baseline verdict is not the answer — use a variant below and re-run.
- The SUT treats each list element as an opaque word; it does not re-segment or strip whitespace *inside* a word (row 14). If word normalization is intended, that is a separate contract change.
- Row 15 is a stability/sanity check, not a performance benchmark; no latency/throughput guarantees are asserted.
- Design-only: correctness of an actual SUT is not established here until the battery is executed against a real implementation.

**Documented variants (alternatives to the baseline):**
1. **Case-insensitive sort** — order by `word.lower()` (or casefold), typically with a stable tie-break on the original string. Under this variant, row 5's expected output changes (e.g., `apple Banana Banana`). Would require re-authoring Tier A expected strings for case-sensitive rows.
2. **Locale-aware / collation sort** — order by a locale collation (e.g., ICU/`locale` collate). Diacritic and case behavior differ from code points (row 8 changes). Less reproducible across environments (locale-dependent), which is why it is not the baseline.
3. **Whitespace-normalizing variant** — if the contract instead required stripping/normalizing whitespace within words or allowing a trailing space, the output contract in §2 and the strict-equality criterion in §6 would both change.

Each variant is a controlled change to §1/§2 definitions; the test structure, controls, and analysis plan carry over unchanged, with only the affected Tier A expected strings re-derived.

---

*This is an experiment design only. No experiment has been executed and no results are claimed.*

Wrapper CLI opcional: lee una línea de `stdin` (palabras separadas por espacios) o usa `argv`, para poder probarlo sin escribir archivos. `split()` sin argumentos maneja cualquier combinación de espacios/entornos de línea.
2. **Ordenación** — `sorted(words, key=KEY)` con Timsort (estable, O(n log n)). La **clave KEY es la única decisión de diseño sustancial**: propongo por defecto `str.lower` (insensible a mayúsculas, estable para empates) sobre Unicode sin normalización; alternativas se listan abajo.
3. **Devolución** — `" ".join(ordenadas)`: exactamente una línea, espacios simples entre palabras, sin espacios al inicio/final. Entrada vacía → línea vacía.

- **Acentos/idioma**: Python ordena por punto de código Unicode, no por colación de idioma. Para español, "ñ" y acentos quedan fuera de un "alfabético" estricto. Opciones: (a) punto de código crudo (simple, reproducible — mi propuesta), (b) normalización NFC antes de ordenar, (c) colación por locale (frágil, no portable → la descarto).
- **Duplicados**: propongo **conservarlos todos**; la estabilidad de Timsort preserva su orden original. (Alternativa: deduplicar — no la propongo.)
- **Palabras vacías/whitespace**: `split()` las elimina; entrada completamente vacía → salida línea vacía.
- **Tamaño de la entrada**: sin restricción declarada; asumida en memoria (lista completa). Timsort escala bien; la verificación de rendimiento cubre hasta 10⁶ palabras si se desea.

payload.answer:
# Diseño final del experimento: programa de ordenación alfabética de palabras

## 1. Contratos: función pura y wrapper CLI

**Función pura (entregable principal):**
```
sort_words(words: list[str]) -> str
```
- **Entrada:** lista de cadenas (ya tokenizadas, o lista vacía).
- **Salida:** una sola cadena con las palabras ordenadas separadas por un espacio simple. **No agrega newline.**
- **Implementación de referencia:** `return " ".join(sorted(words, key=KEY))`.
- **Semántica de newline:** la función es pura respecto al texto: el resultado es exactamente la línea, sin `\n`.

**Wrapper CLI (interfaz de prueba, opcional):**
```
python3 sort_program.py < entrada.txt   # o: echo "b a c" | python3 sort_program.py
```
- **Canal de entrada:** `sys.stdin` (una línea, palabras separadas por cualquier whitespace) o, si `argv` tiene argumentos, los usa como palabras.
- **Procesamiento:** `words = sys.stdin.read().split()` (o `sys.argv[1:]`); `sys.stdout.write(sort_words(words) + "\n")`.
- **Canal de salida:** `stdout` con **un newline final** (convención Unix). `stderr` reservado para errores; salida de éxito siempre es exactamente una línea.

## 2. Clave de ordenación elegida y justificación

**KEY = `str.lower`** aplicada sobre el texto **sin normalización Unicode** (punto de código crudo).
- *Justificación de `str.lower`:* hace el ordenamiento insensible a mayúsculas, lo que coincide con la intuición de "alfabético" para entradas mixtas (`Banana, apple, Cherry` → `apple Banana Cherry`); al ser Timsort estable, los empates tras la clave conservan el orden original de la lista de entrada (determinismo total).
- *Justificación de sin normalización:* máxima simplicidad y reproducibilidad entre plataformas; `str.lower` en Python es determinista. Se documenta como limitación: acentos y `ñ` se ordenan por punto de código (p. ej., `ñandú` tras `z`), no por colación de idioma. La normalización NFC queda registrada como extensión opcional no incluida en la línea base.

## 3. Decisiones de casos límite (fijas)

| Caso | Decisión |
|---|---|
| Duplicados | **Conservar todos**; estabilidad de Timsort preserva su orden relativo original. Sin deduplicación. |
| Entrada vacía (lista `[]` o stdin sin palabras) | La función devuelve `""` (cadena vacía); el wrapper escribe una **línea vacía** (`"\n"`). |
| Separación irregular | `split()` sin argumentos: cualquier combinación de espacios, tabuladores y saltos de línea; nunca produce tokens vacíos. |
| Newline final | Función pura: **no**. Wrapper CLI: **sí** (una sola línea en stdout). |

## 4. Controles

**Tabla de casos unitarios** (cada fila: entrada → salida esperada; esperadas calculadas con la KEY definida):

| # | Caso | Entrada | Salida esperada |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ya ordenada | `["apple", "banana", "cherry"]` | `apple banana cherry` |
| 2 | Invertida | `["cherry", "banana", "apple"]` | `apple banana cherry` |
| 3 | Todas iguales | `["kiwi", "kiwi", "kiwi"]` | `kiwi kiwi kiwi` |
| 4 | Duplicados mezclados | `["pear", "apple", "pear", "apple"]` | `apple apple pear pear` |
| 5 | Mezcla de mayúsculas | `["Banana", "apple", "Cherry", "APPLE"]` | `apple APPLE Banana Cherry` |
| 6 | Acentos / ñ | `["ñandú", "Norte", "ana", "zorro"]` | `ana Norte zorro ñandú` |
| 7 | Lista vacía | `[]` | `""` (wrapper: línea vacía) |
| 8 | Palabra única | `["solo"]` | `solo` |
| 9 | Espacios irregulares (CLI) | `"  b   a\t\n c  "` | `a b c` |

**Tres invariantes** (se verifican sobre los 9 casos y sobre entradas generadas aleatoriamente):
1. **Multiconjunto igual:** `sorted(salida.split()) == sorted(entrada)` — ninguna palabra se pierde, duplica o altera.
2. **No decreciente según KEY:** para todo par vecino, `KEY(salida[i]) <= KEY(salida[i+1])`.
3. **Formato de línea:** la salida contiene exactamente una línea, sin espacios al inicio/final y sin dobles espacios (equivalente a `salida == " ".join(salida.split())`, salvo el caso vacío).

## 5. Plan de análisis

- **Oráculo cruzado 1 (misma KEY):** ejecutar `sorted(words, key=str.lower)` de forma independiente (implementación de referencia separada del wrapper) y comparar con la salida de `sort_words`. Detecta errores de cableado (join, newline, canal stdin/stdout).
- **Oráculo cruzado 2 (variante por punto de código):** para validar la base de ordenamiento crudo, comparar contra `LC_ALL=C sort` de la shell (que ordena por bytes/punto de código) usando una versión de la clave sin `str.lower` (`key=None`). Esto aísla el efecto de `str.lower` del orden subyacente.
- **Métrica de comparación:** **coincidencia exacta de secuencia** (string igual, carácter a carácter, incl. ausencia de espacios extra). Sin métricas aproximadas.
- **Criterio de éxito:** **100% de los casos pasan** (9/9 unitarios + todas las invariantes + coincidencia exacta con ambos oráculos en sus variantes correspondientes). Cualquier desviación = fallo; se documenta y se itera antes de dar por cerrado el diseño.
- **Verificación de rendimiento (opcional, solo si se requiere escalar):** medir con n = 10², 10⁴, 10⁶ para confirmar crecimiento ~n log n; no es parte del criterio de éxito principal.

## 6. Viabilidad

- **Runtime:** Python 3.14.4 de sistema (verificado con `python3 --version`); solo **stdlib** (`sorted`, `sys`, `str`) — sin dependencias externas, compatible con el entorno sin red y sin paquetes preinstalados.
- **Recursos:** O(n log n) tiempo, O(n) memoria; sin GPU, sin datasets, sin I/O de red; la entrada cabe en memoria.
- **Consistencia con la tarea:** `task.json`/`track.md` declaran "Design-only task" — este documento es el entregable; **no se ejecutó ningún experimento** y ningún resultado se afirma aquí.
- **Repositorio:** `/workspace` contiene únicamente `task.json`; no hay código previo ni fixtures que el diseño deba respetar, por lo que el contrato propuesto es libre de restricciones existentes.

Ninguno de estos hallazgos contradice el diseño: todo el plan usa únicamente stdlib (sorted, sys, str) y no requiere cómputo, red ni archivos de datos.
